extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics instructors (professors, lecturers) seeking assessment methods
extracted.subtask_description: Practical methods and evaluation criteria for assessing undergraduate mathematics students using writing (portfolios, journals, short papers), weekly questions, group assignments, and group tests; includes weighting schemes, timing, and grading heuristics. Focused on classroom implementation and instructor practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio evaluation: correctness primary; writing/organization secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: I evaluate the portfolio primarily on correctness of solutions and secondarily on writing and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each portfolio entry should include the problem statement and its detailed solution, including relevant diagrams. Portfolios may consist of traditional problems but creative presentations (cartoons, prefatory material) are acceptable. Provide feedback via rough-draft submissions and provisional grades to guide final work. Instructor changed weighting to give writing/portfolio equal weight with tests/homework after observing student effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio content requirement: problem + detailed solution + diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolio items should include the problem (or description of task) and its detailed solution, including relevant diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly require full solutions and supporting diagrams so the instructor can assess both mathematical correctness and the student's exposition. Portfolios can include student-created graphs or graphs taken from publications; narrative/contextual explanations (e.g., newspaper-style articles, poems, lesson plans) are acceptable as long as the mathematical content and solution are clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rough drafts and provisional grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage students to turn in rough drafts (e.g., the weekend before the Friday due date) so the instructor can make suggestions and corrections without pressure to assign final grades immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors may assign provisional grades on drafts to give students a sense of preliminary quality. This provides formative feedback and improves final submissions. Use draft rounds to correct misconceptions before final grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting writing equally with tests and homework
rubrics_metrics.description: After observing student effort and the insight gained from their writing, assign writing assignments and the portfolio equal weight with tests and homework in the final course grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor initially counted writing collectively as 10% but revised to equal weighting after finding students devoted more thought to writing and it revealed student thinking. Be prepared to justify weights to students and reflect them in the syllabus and midterm reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal policy: not graded but regularly reviewed
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals are not graded for points; they are a personal record of mathematical experiences intended to foster reflection and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require entries at least once a week. Collect journals every two or three weeks and return them within a week. Offer no strict length guidelines; allow some entries unrelated to mathematics. Correct grammar and spelling and comment on content (questions, references, praise) but avoid assigning a grade to preserve candid reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals as formative dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Use journals as a form of self-assessment and an opportunity for dialogue between student and teacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use instructor comments to prompt further thinking; entries made before discussion can act as rehearsals for participation, while entries after class are reflections. Treat journals as part of ongoing conversation rather than summative assessment to encourage risk-taking and exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short papers: length, scoring tiers, and originality heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Weekly short (approximately 250-word) essays count a small number of points toward the final grade and are scored on tiers: skimpy (2 points), typical/check (3 points), and 'check plus' for special insight (4 points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syllabus guidance: 'You may explore ideas further (if you want an ‘A’) or merely summarize the author’s comments (if you are content with a ‘B–’).' Apply lateness penalties flexibly (no rigid algorithm) to account for legitimate reasons. Determining originality is often straightforward—reward exploration, independent learning, and substantive critique with the higher tier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly reading questions: submission and point credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Require students to hand in questions about the assigned reading at the beginning of each week; each question counts one point toward the final grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures students have read the material and provides raw material for in-class discussion. Use submitted questions to guide lesson planning and to identify topics that require more exposition. Consider awarding extra credit/points for questions that show deeper curiosity or lead to substantive class discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-paper grading: examples and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Short papers serve to reveal student understanding and misconceptions and are useful for instructor feedback and class discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read and comment on at least one paper per student (or write a comment about the content), read exemplary excerpts aloud anonymously to create intrinsic reward, and use papers to identify confusions to be addressed in class. Papers that merely summarize still inform teaching but are less likely to receive 'check plus' credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course-grade weighting including group component (example distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a multi-component grade that includes individual tests, quizzes, final exam, group projects, and participation. Example distribution: 3 tests 30%, 4 quizzes 10%, final exam 20%, group projects 30%, participation 10%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust weights to reflect course goals; the example emphasizes group work (about 45% of course in some midsemester calculations). Communicate weights in the syllabus and midterm reports so students understand how grades are computed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midsemester report and transparency about grade computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide each student a midsemester report showing how points/grades are being allocated and indicating progress (including the portion already earned via group projects/participation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the midterm report to illustrate how individual vs. group components contribute to the grade and to motivate students to participate in group activities. Point out that individual work may count more heavily in the latter part of the semester if that is the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation grade components
rubrics_metrics.description: Define participation to include submission of journal entries each week, preparation for and contributions in class, and group interaction during class and outside class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess participation holistically. Give credit (e.g., checks) for any reasonable weekly journal submission. Include evidence of preparation (e.g., having done readings/problems), quality of contributions, and constructive engagement with group members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group test design: independent problems and single-group submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Design group tests with completely independent problems so groups may start anywhere; each group submits one solution per problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make group tests somewhat longer and harder than individual tests so no one individual could finish it in the hour. Encourage groups to plan test-taking strategies in advance (e.g., split problems among members, allow quiet thinking time). Hold a review problem session before the test. Use group tests early to promote group interaction, reduce first-test tension, and prevent withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly group assignments: frequency and grading
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign challenging group problems regularly (often weekly) and grade them almost every week as part of the group project component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use weekly grading to maintain steady group engagement and to provide frequent feedback. Group work may vary by course (e.g., computer algebra lab tasks for calculus/discrete math; proof-writing emphasis for abstract algebra/topology). Reading group submissions weekly lets instructor detect common weaknesses quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals credited toward participation with liberal crediting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the journal submissions as one component of participation credit by giving 'any reasonable submission' a check toward the participation grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond in journals without assigning a grade; use journal entries diagnostically to address group dynamics or personal issues affecting participation. Allow journals to be low-stakes but regularly credited to encourage consistent reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using group work to identify and remediate common errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and analyze groups' weekly work to identify widespread misunderstandings (e.g., incorrect reuse of a single existential integer in multiple cases) and address them promptly in class or follow-up exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a common error is detected, design an in-class activity or homework that targets the misconception, revisit the relevant theory, and provide counterexamples or guided practice. Use group visits to office hours and journal discussions to further diagnose and remediate problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication of assessment plan and cooperative-learning expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the assessment plan and cooperative-learning structure at the beginning of the course and include test dates and relative weights in the syllabus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early, transparent communication helps motivate students to participate and avoids misunderstandings later. Reinforce the plan at midterm when giving reports so students understand the balance between group and individual assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group exam support practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Support group exams with preparatory practices: review problem sessions, advising groups to plan strategies, and instructing individuals to take quiet thinking time before group discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices increase the efficacy of group exams and help groups allocate tasks efficiently during the exam. Consider occasional bonus points for groups that show significant improvement or excellence.
